newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada anti-smoking law seen facing stiff test.
newsitem.headline: Canada anti-smoking law seen facing stiff test.

text.p: As Canada's three big tobacco firms prepare to challenge the legality of the federal government's strict new anti-smoking law, some legal analysts doubt the measure will survive a constitutional test.

Rothmans Benson and Hedges Inc., RJR-Macdonald Inc. and Imperial Tobacco Inc. will argue before the Quebec Superior Court on May 26 that Canada's Tobacco Act is unconstitutional because it violates free speech guarantees.

The law, which took effect on April 25, is considered one of the world's toughest anti-smoking measures. The Canadian Supreme Court struck down a similar 1995 law on grounds it infringed the right of free speech.

Anti-tobacco crusaders contend there is ample evidence to prove tobacco advertising leads to tobacco-related deaths and that the new law meets the constitutional requirement that any restriction on free speech serve the public interest.
The latest measure bans tobacco advertising in stores and on billboards. Violations are punishable by fines of up to C$300,000 ($216,000) or up to two years in jail.
Amid public pressure, the government amended the law to allow tobacco sponsorship of sporting and cultural events until Oct. 1, 1998.
A Quebec court last month denied a bid by the tobacco companies for an injunction against the law until its constitutionality was tested.
University of Ottawa law professor Joseph Magnet said a constitutional challenge to the act would not be frivolous.
"There are serious constitutional problems with the act," said Magnet. "The (government) has skated on some very thin ice."

Neil Finkelstein, a constitutional lawyer for the Toronto law firm Blake Cassels and Graydon, said: "I think there is a very strong case to be made that the provisions concerning sponsorship are unconstitutional.
"I think it is obvious -- the government should know it," Finkelstein said.
A legal defeat for the new law would be a huge setback for Canadian anti-tobacco crusaders.

Canadian activists, who have focused on pressuring governments to regulate tobacco, may need to start suing the tobacco industry, said Janice Forsythe, executive director of the Canadian Council on Smoking and Health.
"We rely on the government to do a lot of the policy things," said Forsythe. "Perhaps we put to many of our eggs in one basket. It is a comprehensive approach that can win this."
Four Ontario smokers have already filed a lawsuit against the Canadian tobacco industry. They hope to turn the suit into a class action and are seeking C$1 million ($720,000) each.
Imperial Tobacco Ltd. is a unit of Montreal-based Imasco Ltd. and controls about 65 percent of the Canadian cigarette market. Imasco is 40 percent-owned by B.A.T. Industries Plc of Britain.

Rothmans, Benson and Hedges Inc., is 60 percent-owned by Rothmans International, a unit of Rothmans International Plc. RIN_u.L and 40 percent by Philip Morris Cos. Inc.. RJR MacDonald is wholly owned by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. unit R.J. Reynolds Tobacco International.
